prompt: You are finishing an expense report late at night, and padding a few receipts would be easy and probably never noticed. You start telling yourself that no one in your position could resist, and that this pressure is unlike anything anyone else faces. What does 1 Corinthians 10:13 counsel here?
options: Accept that your temptation is unique to you and too strong to resist, so a small lapse is understandable
Remember that this temptation is common to man, and that God is faithful to provide a way to escape so you can bear it
Give in this once, since God sometimes allows people to be tempted beyond what they are able to bear
Conclude that God has left you alone in this, so you must decide entirely on your own strength
explanation: 1 Corinthians 10:13 teaches that no temptation is beyond what is common to man, and that God is faithful and will with the temptation make a way to escape. The passage rules out both the 'unique' excuse and the idea that God allows unbearable temptation.
hint: The verse speaks about how ordinary temptation is and about God's faithfulness in the midst of it.
kjv: There hath no temptation taken you but such as is common to man: but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted above that ye are able; but will with the temptation also make a way to escape, that ye may be able to bear it.

prompt: You run a small home bakery, and customers rarely check whether a 'one-pound' bag actually weighs a pound. Shaving a little off each order would quietly boost your profits. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 11:1?
options: Trim the portions slightly, since customers never weigh them and no one is harmed
Keep weights honest only for regular customers who might notice
Give honest measure every time, because a just weight is the LORD's delight and a false balance is an abomination to him
Lower the weight but add a nicer label so customers feel they still got value
explanation: Proverbs 11:1 says a false balance is abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight. Honest measure matters whether or not anyone checks.
hint: Think about what the verse says the LORD delights in when it comes to measuring.
kjv: A false balance is abomination to the LORD: but a just weight is his delight.

prompt: At your office, coworkers casually take printer paper, pens and snacks home, and the amounts seem trivial. You wonder whether small things like this really matter for a person of integrity. Which response best reflects the teaching of Luke 16:10?
options: Be faithful even in these small things, because the one faithful in what is least is faithful also in much
Small items do not count; integrity only matters when large sums are involved
Take what you need now and plan to be honest later when you have more responsibility
Follow whatever your coworkers do, since shared habits cannot be dishonest
keywords: faithful in that which is least
explanation: Luke 16:10 teaches that he that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much, and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. Small choices reveal and shape character.
hint: The verse connects how we handle little things with how we handle big ones.
kjv: He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much.

prompt: Late in the evening you read a cutting message from a colleague, and you have a blistering reply drafted and ready to send. No one would stop you, and it would feel satisfying in the moment. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 25:28?
options: Send it immediately, since expressing every feeling is a sign of strength
Send it but copy others so the colleague feels publicly corrected
Let your feelings have free rein tonight and deal with any damage tomorrow
Rule your own spirit and hold back, because a person without self-control is like a city broken down and without walls
explanation: Proverbs 25:28 compares a man that hath no rule over his own spirit to a city that is broken down and without walls. Lack of self-control leaves a person exposed and vulnerable.
hint: The verse uses the picture of a city's defenses to describe self-control.
kjv: He that hath no rule over his own spirit is like a city that is broken down, and without walls.

prompt: You find a wallet full of cash in an empty parking lot, and the thought of keeping it grows stronger the longer you hold it. You catch yourself thinking, 'God must have put this in my path to test me, so it's partly on Him.' What does James 1:13-15 counsel here?
options: Treat the situation as God tempting you, so the responsibility is shared
Assume that a thought which is only entertained privately can never lead anywhere harmful
Recognize that God tempts no one; you are drawn away by your own desire, and desire that is allowed to grow brings forth sin
Keep the cash, since finding it without witnesses proves it was meant for you
keywords: drawn away of his own lust
explanation: James 1:13-15 says God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man; rather every man is tempted when he is drawn away of his own lust and enticed, and lust when it hath conceived bringeth forth sin. Blame cannot be shifted to God, and inner desire left unchecked grows into sin.
hint: The passage traces temptation to its true source and describes how it grows.
kjv: Let no man say when he is tempted, I am tempted of God: for God cannot be tempted with evil, neither tempteth he any man: But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. Then when lust hath conceived, it bringeth forth sin: and sin, when it is finished, bringeth forth death.

prompt: Weeks ago you made an error in a report that cost your team time, and no one ever traced it back to you. You could keep quiet forever, or you could come clean and change how you work. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 28:13?
options: Confess the mistake and forsake the careless habit, for whoever confesses and forsakes their sins will find mercy
Stay silent, since covering a mistake that no one discovered is the wisest way to prosper
Quietly blame the error on a system glitch so no one is hurt
Admit it only if someone else discovers it first
explanation: Proverbs 28:13 teaches that he that covereth his sins shall not prosper, but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy. Concealment is the path the verse warns against.
hint: The verse contrasts two responses to wrongdoing and the outcome of each.
kjv: He that covereth his sins shall not prosper: but whoso confesseth and forsaketh them shall have mercy.

prompt: You work remotely, and you notice you only work hard when your manager's status shows online or a check-in call is coming up. The rest of the time you coast, confident no one can tell. Which response best reflects the teaching of Colossians 3:22?
options: Work diligently mainly when your supervisor is watching, since pleasing them is the goal of good work
Coast when unobserved, because obedience only applies to tasks someone checks
Put effort into looking busy on camera so your manager feels reassured
Work with singleness of heart, fearing God, rather than with eyeservice as a menpleaser
explanation: Colossians 3:22 calls for work not with eyeservice, as menpleasers, but in singleness of heart, fearing God. Working hard only when observed is exactly the eyeservice the verse rejects.
hint: Look for the unusual word the verse uses for work done only to be seen.
kjv: Servants, obey in all things your masters according to the flesh; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but in singleness of heart, fearing God:

prompt: Your family is away for the weekend, and you are alone at home with a streaming service and an internet browser. Some content you would never watch in front of others is just a click away. Which response best reflects the teaching of Psalms 101:2-3?
options: Integrity is for public life; what you watch in private at home is a separate matter
Walk within your house with a perfect heart and set no wicked thing before your eyes
Watch it this once, so long as you resolve to behave wisely in public afterward
Allow yourself a little, since only outward deeds, not what you look at, can cleave to you
keywords: no wicked thing before mine eyes
explanation: In Psalms 101:2-3 the psalmist resolves, 'I will walk within my house with a perfect heart. I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes.' Integrity is pledged specifically for private life at home and for what one chooses to look at.
hint: Notice where the psalmist says he will walk with integrity, and what he refuses to look at.
kjv: I will behave myself wisely in a perfect way. O when wilt thou come unto me? I will walk within my house with a perfect heart. I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.

prompt: A coworker's husband died suddenly, and she now lives alone. Several weeks after the funeral, most people have stopped checking on her, and you wonder whether it is your place to reach out. Which response best reflects the teaching of James 1:27?
options: Visit her in her affliction and continue showing practical care, since caring for widows is part of pure religion
Leave her alone, because grief is private and visits only intrude
Send one sympathy card and consider your duty finished, since the funeral is over
Wait for her to ask for help, since it is not your responsibility to visit
explanation: James 1:27 describes pure and undefiled religion as including the duty 'to visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction.' Continuing to visit and care for her lives out that teaching.
hint: Notice what James says pure religion actively does for those who are suffering.
kjv: Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.

prompt: Your close friend has been caring for his elderly father, who has dementia, and he admits he is exhausted and hasn't had a break in months. You have a free Saturday each month. What does Galatians 6:2 counsel here?
options: Tell him that everyone must carry his own family problems alone
Offer to share the load, such as staying with his father so he can rest
Advise him to stop talking about his struggles so he doesn't burden others
Avoid him for a while so his stress doesn't affect you
explanation: Galatians 6:2 commands, 'Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.' Helping carry your friend's caregiving load is a direct application.
hint: The verse speaks of what believers should do with each other's heavy loads.
kjv: Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

prompt: Years ago you lost your mother and were deeply comforted by friends and by your faith. Now a new colleague has just lost her mother and seems overwhelmed. Which response best reflects the teaching of 2 Corinthians 1:3-4?
options: Keep your own loss to yourself, since past sorrow should never be revisited
Tell her that her grief is smaller than yours was, so she should cope
Use the comfort you received from God to comfort her in her trouble
Avoid her until she is feeling better, since comforting is for professionals
keywords: comfort them which are in any trouble
explanation: 2 Corinthians 1:4 says God comforts us 'that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.' Your past comfort equips you to comfort her.
hint: Paul explains a purpose behind the comfort God gives us.
kjv: Blessed be God, even the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies, and the God of all comfort; Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God.

prompt: At a community meeting, an elderly neighbor slowly rises to share a concern, and some younger attendees roll their eyes and talk over him. You are seated nearby. Which response best reflects the teaching of Leviticus 19:32?
options: Join the others in ignoring him, since older people's views are outdated
Interrupt him to speed the meeting along
Treat him as no different from a nuisance, since age earns no special regard
Show him honor and respect, giving him attention as he speaks
keywords: honour the face of the old man
explanation: Leviticus 19:32 commands, 'Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God.' Showing him respect reflects this command.
hint: The verse ties reverence for God to how we treat the aged.
kjv: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.

prompt: Your widowed mother needs help with errands and household needs, but you have been pouring your time into volunteer projects across town and barely see her. You feel pulled in two directions. Which response best reflects the teaching of 1 Timothy 5:4?
options: Learn first to show piety at home by caring for your mother, repaying what your parents gave you
Focus only on outside projects, since helping family earns no credit before God
Assume someone else in the church will handle her needs, so you need not
Tell her she should manage on her own, since adult children owe parents nothing
explanation: 1 Timothy 5:4 says the children of a widow should 'learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.' Caring for your mother is the priority this verse describes.
hint: Paul says something should be learned 'first' and where it should be practiced.
kjv: But if any widow have children or nephews, let them learn first to shew piety at home, and to requite their parents: for that is good and acceptable before God.

prompt: A friend's teenage son has died, and you go to the house unsure what to say. You feel pressure to explain the tragedy or offer advice. Which response best reflects the example of Job's friends in Job 2:11-13?
options: Explain at length why this must have happened so your friend can understand
Stay away until you have the right words, since silence is unhelpful
Come and sit with your friend in his grief, sharing quiet presence rather than many words
Quickly change the subject to lighter topics so he forgets his pain
explanation: Job's friends came 'to mourn with him and to comfort him' and 'sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great' (Job 2:11-13). Their silent presence is the example in this passage.
hint: Look at what the friends did before anyone began to speak.
kjv: Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that was come upon him, they came every one from his own place; Eliphaz the Temanite, and Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite: for they had made an appointment together to come to mourn with him and to comfort him. And when they lifted up their eyes afar off, and knew him not, they lifted up their voice, and wept; and they rent every one his mantle, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven. So they sat down with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him: for they saw that his grief was very great.

prompt: A friend is deeply grieving a recent loss, and you plan to visit. You're tempted to arrive with upbeat music and jokes to 'snap her out of it.' Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 25:20?
options: Insist on cheerfulness, because forced joy quickly cures sorrow
Be gentle and sensitive to her heavy heart rather than pressing lighthearted cheer on her
Tell her that grieving shows weak faith and she should sing instead
Bring a group for a party so she has no time to feel sad
explanation: Proverbs 25:20 compares one 'that singeth songs to an heavy heart' to taking away a garment in cold weather and 'vinegar upon nitre.' Forced cheer wounds rather than comforts, so gentleness fits the moment.
hint: Consider the images of a removed coat in winter and a harsh reaction.
kjv: As he that taketh away a garment in cold weather, and as vinegar upon nitre, so is he that singeth songs to an heavy heart.

prompt: On the same evening, you are invited to a lively celebration with friends and to the visitation for a coworker's elderly father who has died. You're inclined to skip the visitation because it feels heavy. Which response best reflects the teaching of Ecclesiastes 7:2?
options: Choose the celebration, since feasting is always wiser than mourning
Skip both, because neither event has anything to teach you
Attend the celebration and avoid thinking about death, since it is not your concern
Go to the house of mourning, where the living reflect on the end of all men
explanation: Ecclesiastes 7:2 says, 'It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.' Attending the visitation honors the grieving and encourages sober reflection.
hint: The Preacher compares two kinds of houses and says which is better.
kjv: It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to go to the house of feasting: for that is the end of all men; and the living will lay it to his heart.

prompt: You've just been promoted to lead your department, and a colleague jokes that now you'll finally have people to do your errands. You wonder what kind of leader you want to be. Which response best reflects the teaching of Mark 10:43-44?
options: See the role as a reward and expect the team to serve your needs first
See greatness in the role as becoming the team's servant and meeting their needs
Keep your distance from the team so they respect your new authority
Use the promotion mainly to get your own ideas recognized
explanation: Jesus taught that whoever would be great 'shall be your minister' and whoever would be chiefest 'shall be servant of all' (Mark 10:43-44). True leadership is measured by service, not by being served.
hint: Jesus turned the usual idea of greatness upside down.
kjv: But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: And whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all.

prompt: A friend from your small group is overwhelmed after losing a job while caring for a sick parent. You have some free evenings and could help with meals and errands. What does Galatians 6:2 counsel here?
options: Wait for them to ask, since everyone should handle their own problems privately
Offer advice from a distance but avoid getting involved in their practical needs
Step in to help carry the load, since this fulfils the law of Christ
Remind them that hardship builds character and leave them to grow through it
explanation: Galatians 6:2 says, 'Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.' Practically sharing a friend's load is how believers live out Christ's law.
hint: The verse speaks of carrying something together.
kjv: Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

prompt: Your team is choosing who will present a successful project to senior leadership, and you know you could push to take the spotlight. A quieter colleague did much of the groundwork. Which response best reflects Philippians 2:3-4?
options: Make sure leadership knows the success was mostly your doing
Stay silent and let credit fall wherever it happens to land, even if it lands on you
Insist on presenting, since visibility is important for your career
Value your colleague above yourself and look out for their interests by giving them the credit and opportunity
explanation: Philippians 2:3-4 teaches to do nothing 'through strife or vainglory' but in 'lowliness of mind' to esteem others better than ourselves, looking 'on the things of others.' Elevating a colleague's contribution fits that humility.
hint: Think about whose interests the passage asks you to look at.
kjv: Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.

prompt: You sit on a neighborhood council deciding how to allocate a small grant. Several low-income families who would be affected aren't at the meeting and have no one representing their needs. Which response best reflects Proverbs 31:8-9?
options: Speak up on their behalf, judge fairly, and plead the cause of the poor and needy
Stay quiet, since those who didn't attend gave up their say
Support whichever option the most influential members prefer
Postpone any decision indefinitely to avoid controversy
explanation: Proverbs 31:8-9 instructs, 'Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.' Those with a voice in decisions should use it for those who lack one.
hint: The passage tells someone in authority what to do with their mouth.
kjv: Open thy mouth for the dumb in the cause of all such as are appointed to destruction. Open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.

prompt: As a supervisor, you're frustrated that a staff member keeps missing deadlines. You're tempted to threaten their job in front of the team to scare everyone into line. Which response best reflects the teaching of Ephesians 6:9?
options: Use threats freely, since fear is an effective motivator
Treat them fairly without threatening, remembering you too answer to a Master in heaven who shows no partiality
Ignore the problem entirely so you never have to confront anyone
Be harsh with this employee but lenient with your favorites
explanation: Ephesians 6:9 tells masters to treat those under them well, 'forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him.' Leaders are accountable to God and must not rule by intimidation or favoritism.
hint: The verse reminds those in charge that they also have someone over them.
kjv: And, ye masters, do the same things unto them, forbearing threatening: knowing that your Master also is in heaven; neither is there respect of persons with him.

prompt: You've been asked to coordinate the volunteer team at your church's food pantry. You feel reluctant and wonder whether you could just give orders while others do the work. What does 1 Peter 5:2-3 counsel here?
options: Accept the role only if it brings recognition or some benefit
Take the role reluctantly and do the bare minimum because you were pressured
Run the team firmly as its boss, since volunteers need to know who's in charge
Serve willingly and eagerly, leading by personal example rather than lording it over others
explanation: 1 Peter 5:2-3 urges oversight 'not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind,' and not as 'lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.' Good leaders serve gladly and lead by example.
hint: The passage contrasts ruling over people with showing them the way.
kjv: Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.

prompt: As a new manager, one employee regularly brings you unflattering stories about coworkers, and you've started acting on them without checking. Office trust is souring. Which response best reflects the warning of Proverbs 29:12?
options: Keep rewarding the informer, since knowing everything strengthens your control
Refuse to listen to falsehoods and verify claims, knowing a leader who heeds lies corrupts the whole team
Share the stories more widely so everyone is aware of the problems
Treat every report as true, since employees wouldn't bother inventing them
explanation: Proverbs 29:12 warns, 'If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked.' A leader who welcomes falsehood encourages it throughout those under him.
hint: Consider what happens to those under a leader when the leader welcomes untrue reports.
kjv: If a ruler hearken to lies, all his servants are wicked.

prompt: You head a small family business through a tough season. One advisor says to rule strictly and conceal hard facts from staff; another says to be kind but always honest. Which response best reflects Proverbs 20:28?
options: Lead with mercy and truth together, since this is what upholds a leader's position
Rely on strict control and fear, since kindness looks weak in hard times
Hide the bad news to keep morale up, even if it means misleading people
Be honest but harsh, since mercy has no place in running a business
explanation: Proverbs 20:28 says, 'Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.' Lasting authority rests on combining compassion with honesty, not fear or deception.
hint: The verse names two qualities that preserve a ruler.
kjv: Mercy and truth preserve the king: and his throne is upholden by mercy.

prompt: Your calendar is crammed with work deadlines, family events, and volunteer commitments, and you feel guilty that you can't do everything at once. A friend suggests you simply accept that different things have their proper times. Which response best reflects the teaching of Ecclesiastes 3:1?
options: Recognize that there is a season and a time for each purpose, and give each task its proper time
Try to do every task simultaneously so nothing ever waits
Conclude that timing doesn't matter and everything should be done immediately
Drop all commitments, since no activity has a rightful place in life
explanation: Ecclesiastes 3:1 teaches that "to every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven." Life's activities each have their fitting time, so not everything must happen at once.
hint: The verse speaks of seasons, not of doing everything at once.
kjv: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven:

prompt: It has been a frustrating week: your car needed repairs and a project at work stalled. Over dinner, you notice you've only talked about what went wrong. What does 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18 counsel here?
options: Wait to give thanks until circumstances improve
Rejoice, keep praying, and give thanks in every thing
Give thanks only for the things that went well this week
Keep a careful record of complaints so you can pray about them later
explanation: 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18 says, "Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks," calling believers to gratitude in all circumstances, not only good ones.
hint: Notice how broadly the passage applies thankfulness.
kjv: Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you.

prompt: At a milestone birthday, you realize years have slipped by while you've postponed what matters most to you. You want to use your remaining time well. Which response best reflects the prayer of Psalms 90:12?
options: Avoid thinking about the passing of time so it doesn't trouble you
Assume there will always be more years, so priorities can wait
Ask God to teach you to number your days so you apply your heart to wisdom
Fill every remaining day with as much activity as possible, regardless of purpose
explanation: Psalms 90:12 prays, "So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom." Being mindful that our days are limited is meant to lead us toward wise living.
hint: The psalmist wants counting days to lead somewhere.
kjv: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.

prompt: You are hosting a dinner and become irritated that a relative is sitting and listening to a guest's stories instead of helping in the kitchen. You're tempted to complain publicly. What does Jesus' response in Luke 10:40-42 suggest?
options: Insist that serving is always more important than listening
Ask the guest to step in and order the relative to help
Conclude that hospitality is unimportant and should be abandoned
Notice that you may be careful and troubled about many things, while one thing is needful
explanation: In Luke 10:40-42 Jesus tells Martha she is "careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful," and that Mary "hath chosen that good part," sitting and hearing his word.
hint: Jesus did not tell the listening sister to get up.
kjv: But Martha was cumbered about much serving, and came to him, and said, Lord, dost thou not care that my sister hath left me to serve alone? bid her therefore that she help me. And Jesus answered and said unto her, Martha, Martha, thou art careful and troubled about many things: But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her.

prompt: You've been staying up past midnight and waking before dawn, convinced that if you just work harder you can secure everything yourself. You are exhausted and anxious. Which response best reflects the teaching of Psalms 127:2?
options: Recognize that anxious overwork is vain and that God gives his beloved sleep
Cut sleep further, since rest is a sign of laziness
Rise even earlier, because success depends entirely on your effort
Eat the bread of sorrows now so you can enjoy life later
explanation: Psalms 127:2 says, "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Sleep is a gift, not a failure.
hint: The verse calls one pattern 'vain' and names a gift.
kjv: It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.

prompt: Your team has just finished an intense stretch of serving clients, so busy that no one had time even to eat lunch. As the leader, you're deciding what to do next. Which response best reflects Jesus' words in Mark 6:31?
options: Schedule another busy stretch immediately to keep momentum
Tell everyone that rest is only for those who did less work
Invite them to come apart to a quiet place and rest a while
Praise the skipped meals as proof of true commitment
explanation: In Mark 6:31 Jesus told his busy disciples, "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while," because "they had no leisure so much as to eat."
hint: Consider what Jesus offered people who had been coming and going nonstop.
kjv: And he said unto them, Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place, and rest a while: for there were many coming and going, and they had no leisure so much as to eat.

prompt: You're offered a promotion with much higher pay, but it would mean constant stress, long hours, and little peace at home. Your current role pays less but leaves room for a calm life. What does Ecclesiastes 4:6 counsel here?
options: Both hands full is always better, whatever the vexation
A handful with quietness is better than both hands full with travail and vexation of spirit
Quietness only matters once you have accumulated plenty
Travail is the surest path to a peaceful spirit
explanation: Ecclesiastes 4:6 says, "Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit," valuing peace above more gain gotten with turmoil.
hint: The verse compares one handful with two, and weighs what comes with each.
kjv: Better is an handful with quietness, than both the hands full with travail and vexation of spirit.

prompt: You've begun working nights and weekends purely to grow your investments, constantly watching market charts and neglecting friendships. A coworker urges you to chase wealth even harder. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 23:4-5?
options: Set your eyes firmly on riches, since they are the most lasting thing
Trust your own cleverness to make sure your riches never leave
Labour all the harder, because wealth stays with those who pursue it
Labour not to be rich, remembering that riches make themselves wings and fly away
explanation: Proverbs 23:4-5 warns, "Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom," because "riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven."
hint: Think about the bird imagery the proverb uses for wealth.
kjv: Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. Wilt thou set thine eyes upon that which is not? for riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven.

prompt: Your teenage nephew is living with you for a year, and you are tempted to leave his character and habits for 'life to sort out later.' You wonder whether patient guidance now really matters. Which response best reflects the teaching of Proverbs 22:6?
options: Assume children will find their own way and that early guidance makes little lasting difference
Wait until he is an adult before trying to shape his habits or values
Leave all guidance to his school, since home life has little effect on character
Take time now to train him in the right way, trusting that early formation tends to last into later life
explanation: Proverbs 22:6 says to 'Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it,' so diligent guidance in youth has lasting value.
hint: Think about what this verse says happens 'when he is old.'
kjv: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.

prompt: Your elderly parents call often, and after a stressful week you are tempted to ignore them and speak dismissively about them to friends. You want to respond rightly. What does Exodus 20:12 counsel here?
options: Honour your father and mother, treating them with respect and regard even when it is inconvenient
Honour your parents only if they have earned it by agreeing with your choices
Keep your distance, since adult children owe their parents nothing further
Speak respectfully to their faces but freely mock them to others
explanation: Exodus 20:12 commands, 'Honour thy father and thy mother,' attaching a promise of long days to the command, with no condition about convenience.
hint: This is one of the Ten Commandments, and the first word of it is a verb about respect.
kjv: Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.

prompt: At a community meeting, an elderly man with white hair slowly makes his way to the front, and some younger attendees roll their eyes and keep their seats. You consider how to respond. Which response best reflects the teaching of Leviticus 19:32?
options: Ignore him, since respect should be based only on someone's position or wealth
Rise and show him honour, treating age itself with respect as an act of reverence toward God
Join the others in quietly laughing at how slow he is
Offer respect only if he proves he is more qualified than the younger speakers
explanation: Leviticus 19:32 says, 'Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God,' tying respect for the aged to reverence for the LORD.
hint: The verse describes a physical action of respect toward grey hair.
kjv: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.

prompt: Your mother, now in her eighties, offers advice about a family matter. Friends say her views are outdated and you should simply tune her out because of her age. What does Proverbs 23:22 counsel here?
options: Stop consulting parents once you have your own household
Listen politely only to your father, since the verse concerns fathers alone
Treat her age as a reason to dismiss her opinions
Listen to your parents and do not despise your mother because she has grown old
explanation: Proverbs 23:22 says, 'Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old,' forbidding contempt for an aging parent.
hint: Notice what the verse says about a mother's age.
kjv: Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old.

prompt: An older volunteer at your organisation has made a real mistake, and you need to address it. A colleague suggests confronting him sharply in front of everyone so he learns his lesson. Which response best reflects the teaching of 1 Timothy 5:1-2?
options: Rebuke him harshly, since age gives no special claim to gentle treatment
Never mention the problem at all, even if it continues
Approach him respectfully and appeal to him as you would to your own father
Ask a younger staff member to scold him publicly so you are not involved
explanation: 1 Timothy 5:1 says, 'Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father,' calling for respectful appeal rather than harsh rebuke, and goes on to treat others as family 'with all purity.'
hint: The passage compares how to treat older and younger people to members of a family.
kjv: Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren; The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.

prompt: Your child keeps failing to finish chores, and you are frustrated. You are tempted to respond with constant belittling and harsh outbursts to 'toughen them up.' Which response best reflects the teaching of Ephesians 6:4?
options: Avoid needlessly provoking them to anger, and instead raise them with patient instruction and godly correction
Use sarcasm and ridicule, since shame is the quickest way to change behaviour
Give up on correction entirely so the child never feels upset
Let the child raise themselves, since instruction is the church's job alone
keywords: provoke not your children to wrath
explanation: Ephesians 6:4 tells fathers to 'provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord,' which rules out both exasperating harshness and abandoning correction.
hint: The verse contains both a warning and a positive instruction for parents.
kjv: And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.

prompt: Your aging father needs some financial help. You are tempted to tell him your money is already pledged to a religious cause, so you are excused from helping him, even though you could do both. In light of Mark 7:10-13, what does Scripture counsel here?
options: A religious pledge rightly cancels any duty to help your parents
Declaring resources set apart as a gift is a wise way to avoid family obligations
Do not use a religious vow as an excuse to neglect your parents, because that makes God's command to honour them of none effect
Honouring parents means only speaking kindly, not practical help
explanation: In Mark 7:10-13 Jesus rebukes those who declared their resources 'Corban' so they need do nothing for father or mother, saying this made 'the word of God of none effect through your tradition.'
hint: Jesus criticised a tradition that used a 'gift' to God as a loophole.
kjv: For Moses said, Honour thy father and thy mother; and, Whoso curseth father or mother, let him die the death: But ye say, If a man shall say to his father or mother, It is Corban, that is to say, a gift, by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me; he shall be free. And ye suffer him no more to do ought for his father or his mother; Making the word of God of none effect through your tradition, which ye have delivered: and many such like things do ye.

prompt: You are the youngest person newly appointed to lead a team, and several older members quietly doubt you because of your age. You wonder how to respond. Which response best reflects the teaching of 1 Timothy 4:12?
options: Demand respect forcefully and remind them often that you are in charge
Become an example in your speech, conduct, love, spirit, faith and purity so your youth gives no cause for contempt
Step aside, since young people should never hold responsibility
Match their attitude by dismissing the older members' contributions
explanation: 1 Timothy 4:12 says, 'Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity,' answering doubts through godly example rather than force.
hint: The verse lists areas of life where a young person should set a pattern.
kjv: Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.

briefing: Shortly after Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai, a group of weary strangers arrives at Joshua's camp in Gilgal. They carry worn-out sacks, patched wineskins and dry, mouldy bread, and they ask for a peace treaty. Investigate Joshua 9 to find out who these travellers really are and what happened.
clue: Camp report: the visitors' sacks are old, their wine bottles torn and bound up, their shoes patched, and all their bread dry and mouldy. Word has it they had heard what Joshua did to Jericho and Ai.
prompt: According to the text, the inhabitants of which town planned this disguise?
options: Gibeon
Jericho
Ai
Gilgal
explanation: Joshua 9:3-5 says the inhabitants of Gibeon 'did work wilily' and came with old sacks, old shoes and mouldy bread. Jericho and Ai were the cities Joshua had already conquered, and Gilgal was Israel's camp (Joshua 9:6).
hint: The plotters had heard about Jericho and Ai, so they were not from either of those cities.
kjv: And when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done unto Jericho and to Ai, They did work wilily, and went and made as if they had been ambassadors, and took old sacks upon their asses, and wine bottles, old, and rent, and bound up; And old shoes and clouted upon their feet, and old garments upon them; and all the bread of their provision was dry and mouldy. And they went to Joshua unto the camp at Gilgal, and said unto him, and to the men of Israel, We be come from a far country: now therefore make ye a league with us.

briefing: Shortly after Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai, a group of weary strangers arrives at Joshua's camp in Gilgal. They bought it at a market in Gilgal
They received it as a gift from the king of Ai
They baked it fresh that morning
explanation: In Joshua 9:12-13 the travellers said they took the bread hot from their houses when they set out, and that it had become dry and mouldy, their bottles torn and clothes worn 'by reason of the very long journey.'

kjv: This our bread we took hot for our provision out of our houses on the day we came forth to go unto you; but now, behold, it is dry, and it is mouldy: And these bottles of wine, which we filled, were new; and, behold, they be rent: and these our garments and our shoes are become old by reason of the very long journey.

briefing: Shortly after Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai, a group of weary strangers arrives at Joshua's camp in Gilgal. clue: Procedure note: the Israelite men examined the visitors' food, and Joshua and the princes swore an oath of peace. One important step was left out.

options: They asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD
They did not taste the visitors' food
They did not let the princes swear
They did not let Joshua make peace

kjv: And the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. And Joshua made peace with them, and made a league with them, to let them live: and the princes of the congregation sware unto them.

briefing: Shortly after Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai, a group of weary strangers arrives at Joshua's camp in Gilgal. They carry worn-out sacks, patched wineskins and dry, mouldy bread, and they ask for a peace treaty. Investigate Joshua 9 to find out who these travellers really are and what happened.
clue: Follow-up report: just three days after the treaty, Israel received news about the strangers and marched to their cities, arriving on the third day.
prompt: What did Israel discover about the travellers?
options: They were neighbours who dwelt among them
They lived beyond the great sea
They came from Egypt
They were Israelites from another tribe
explanation: Joshua 9:16 says Israel heard 'that they were their neighbours, and that they dwelt among them,' and verse 17 names their cities: Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kirjathjearim.
hint: The 'very long journey' turned out to be much shorter than claimed.
kjv: And it came to pass at the end of three days after they had made a league with them, that they heard that they were their neighbours, and that they dwelt among them. And the children of Israel journeyed, and came unto their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, and Chephirah, and Beeroth, and Kirjath-jearim.

briefing: Shortly after Israel's victories at Jericho and Ai, a group of weary strangers arrives at Joshua's camp in Gilgal. They carry worn-out sacks, patched wineskins and dry, mouldy bread, and they ask for a peace treaty. Investigate Joshua 9 to find out who these travellers really are and what happened.
clue: Final interrogation: Joshua asked, 'Wherefore have ye beguiled us?' The Gibeonites gave their reason and placed themselves in his hand.
prompt: Case solved: what really happened, and how did it end?
options: The Gibeonites, sore afraid for their lives, pretended to come from far away; they were spared but made hewers of wood and drawers of water
The Gibeonites were truly from a far country and became Israel's honoured allies
The men of Ai disguised themselves, and Joshua destroyed them
The Gibeonites stole Israel's bread and were driven out of the land
explanation: In Joshua 9:24 the Gibeonites said they 'were sore afraid of our lives' and so 'have done this thing.' Joshua 9:26-27 says he delivered them from being slain and made them hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and the altar of the LORD.
hint: Their lives were spared because of the oath, but their deception had a lasting consequence.
kjv: And Joshua called for them, and he spake unto them, saying, Wherefore have ye beguiled us, saying, We are very far from you; when ye dwell among us? Now therefore ye are cursed, and there shall none of you be freed from being bondmen, and hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God. And they answered Joshua, and said, Because it was certainly told thy servants, how that the LORD thy God commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land, and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you, therefore we were sore afraid of our lives because of you, and have done this thing. And now, behold, we are in thine hand: as it seemeth good and right unto thee to do unto us, do. And so did he unto them, and delivered them out of the hand of the children of Israel, that they slew them not. And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose.

briefing: A man known to have been blind from birth is suddenly seen walking the streets with full sight, and his neighbors cannot agree whether he is even the same man. The religious leaders open an inquiry, questioning the man and his parents. Reconstruct what really happened from the case file of John 9.
clue: Witness report: Jesus and his disciples passed a man blind since birth, and the disciples asked their Master a pointed question about blame.
prompt: According to Jesus, why was this man born blind?
options: Because his parents had sinned
Because the man himself had sinned
So that the works of God should be made manifest in him
Because he had broken the sabbath
explanation: Jesus answered that neither the man nor his parents had sinned, but that the works of God should be made manifest in him (John 9:3).
hint: Jesus rejected both options the disciples suggested.
kjv: And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man which was blind from his birth. And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him.

briefing: A man known to have been blind from birth is suddenly seen walking the streets with full sight, and his neighbors cannot agree whether he is even the same man. clue: Physical evidence: traces of clay made with spittle were applied to the man's eyes, and he was given instructions to go somewhere.
prompt: Where was the man told to go and wash?
options: The river Jordan
The pool of Siloam
The pool of Bethesda
The temple laver
explanation: Jesus anointed the man's eyes with clay and told him, 'Go, wash in the pool of Siloam'; he washed and came seeing (John 9:6-7).

clue: Pharisee testimony: 'This man is not of God,' some of them said of the healer, pointing to the day on which the clay was made.
prompt: On what day did Jesus make the clay and open the man's eyes?

The first day of the week
The sabbath day
The day of atonement
explanation: It was the sabbath day when Jesus made the clay, and some Pharisees said he was not of God because he kept not the sabbath day (John 9:14,16).
hint: Their objection concerned a weekly day of rest.

clue: Statement of the parents: 'We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind... he is of age; ask him.'
prompt: Why did the man's parents refuse to say how their son received his sight?
options: They feared the Jews, who had agreed to put out of the synagogue anyone who confessed Jesus was Christ
They had not seen their son in many years
They believed he had been healed by a physician
They were angry with their son
explanation: His parents spoke this way because they feared the Jews, who had agreed that anyone confessing Jesus as Christ would be put out of the synagogue (John 9:22).
hint: Consider what the text says would happen to anyone who made a certain confession.
kjv: But the Jews did not believe concerning him, that he had been blind, and received his sight, until they called the parents of him that had received his sight. And they asked them, saying, Is this your son, who ye say was born blind? how then doth he now see? His parents answered them and said, We know that this is our son, and that he was born blind: But by what means he now seeth, we know not; or who hath opened his eyes, we know not: he is of age; ask him: he shall speak for himself. These words spake his parents, because they feared the Jews: for the Jews had agreed already, that if any man did confess that he was Christ, he should be put out of the synagogue. Therefore said his parents, He is of age; ask him.

reading_text.text: Another parable put he forth unto them, saying, The kingdom of heaven is likened unto a man which sowed good seed in his field: But while men slept, his enemy came and sowed tares among the wheat, and went his way. But when the blade was sprung up, and brought forth fruit, then appeared the tares also. So the servants of the householder came and said unto him, Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares? He said unto them, An enemy hath done this. The servants said unto him, Wilt thou then that we go and gather them up? But he said, Nay; lest while ye gather up the tares, ye root up also the wheat with them. Let both grow together until the harvest: and in the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather ye together first the tares, and bind them in bundles to burn them: but gather the wheat into my barn.

Then Jesus sent the multitude away, and went into the house: and his disciples came unto him, saying, Declare unto us the parable of the tares of the field. He answered and said unto them, He that soweth the good seed is the Son of man; The field is the world; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; but the tares are the children of the wicked one; The enemy that sowed them is the devil; the harvest is the end of the world; and the reapers are the angels. As therefore the tares are gathered and burned in the fire; so shall it be in the end of this world. The Son of man shall send forth his angels, and they shall gather out of his kingdom all things that offend, and them which do iniquity; And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth. Then shall the righteous shine forth as the sun in the kingdom of their Father. Who hath ears to hear, let him hear.

reading_text.text: And it came to pass, that, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said unto him, Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples. And he said unto them, When ye pray, say, Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done, as in heaven, so in earth. Give us day by day our daily bread. And forgive us our sins; for we also forgive every one that is indebted to us. And lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil. And he said unto them, Which of you shall have a friend, and shall go unto him at midnight, and say unto him, Friend, lend me three loaves; For a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him? And he from within shall answer and say, Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee. I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth. And I say unto you, Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened. If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone? or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent? Or if he shall ask an egg, will he offer him a scorpion? intro: Jesus was eating in the house of a Pharisee named Simon when a woman of the city, known as a sinner, came and anointed His feet. Simon said within himself that a true prophet would know what manner of woman was touching Him, and Jesus answered with this short story addressed to Simon (Luke 7:36-40).
prompt: In Jesus' story, how much did the two debtors owe the creditor?
options: One owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty
One owed a thousand talents, and the other a hundred
Each owed fifty pence
One owed ten pence, and the other one pence
explanation: Jesus said a certain creditor had two debtors: 'the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty' (Luke 7:41).
hint: One debt was ten times the size of the other.
kjv: There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty.

reading_text.text: And one of the Pharisees desired him that he would eat with him. And he went into the Pharisee’s house, and sat down to meat. And, behold, a woman in the city, which was a sinner, when she knew that Jesus sat at meat in the Pharisee’s house, brought an alabaster box of ointment, And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment. Now when the Pharisee which had bidden him saw it, he spake within himself, saying, This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner. And Jesus answering said unto him, Simon, I have somewhat to say unto thee. And he saith, Master, say on. There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty. And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most? Simon answered and said, I suppose that he, to whom he forgave most. And he said unto him, Thou hast rightly judged. And he turned to the woman, and said unto Simon, Seest thou this woman? I entered into thine house, thou gavest me no water for my feet: but she hath washed my feet with tears, and wiped them with the hairs of her head. Thou gavest me no kiss: but this woman since the time I came in hath not ceased to kiss my feet. My head with oil thou didst not anoint: but this woman hath anointed my feet with ointment. Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little. And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven. And they that sat at meat with him began to say within themselves, Who is this that forgiveth sins also? And he said to the woman, Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace.
